I prepared the initial dichromatic pattern using the **actual GB geometry**, not the nearby exact Σ9 geometry.

![Initial FCC Ni dichromatic pattern](artifacts/structure/dichromatic_map/dichromatic-map-20260927-051048-fb4d97/dichromatic_map.png)

## Setup

- Lattice: FCC Ni
- Lattice parameter: \(a_0=3.52\) Å
- Actual misorientation: \(35.26438968^\circ\)
- Tilt axis: \([1\bar{1}0]\)
- Grain 1/top plane: \((110)\), blue
- Grain 2/bottom plane: \((111)\), orange
- Axial period: \(0.707107a_0\)
- Two axial layers, A and B
- Layer spacing: \(0.353553a_0\)
- Display region: \(12a_0\times12a_0\)
- Visible atoms: 409 per grain
- Exact visible coincidences: 1
- Local near-coincident pairs: 12
- Candidate sites available for later inspection: 13

The nearby Σ9 branch at \(38.94244127^\circ\) was retained only as descriptive context and was **not** substituted for the actual \(35.26438968^\circ\) boundary.

### Important limitation

No exact CSL cell was found at the actual angle within the bounded rational search. This is therefore an **ideal, unstrained dichromatic projection**, not a primitive three-dimensional periodic cell or a relaxed GB structure. Coincidences and near-pairs are compared within the same axial phase.

No strain, four-point selection, cell construction, or atomic relaxation was performed.

- Dichromatic-map run: `dichromatic-map-20260927-051048-fb4d97`
- Setup run: `csl-20260927-051042-490db6`
- [Numerical map data](artifacts/structure/dichromatic_map/dichromatic-map-20260927-051048-fb4d97/dichromatic_map.json)

The next optional step would be an interactive four-point selection from this map to define a candidate near-coincident cell; that selection should be made explicitly rather than inferred automatically.
